paras: The lynching of Andrew Jackson was the killing of a Black man by a mob in early November 1882, reported as having taken place near Vienna, in Lincoln Parish, Louisiana. Jackson was accused of assaulting a white girl, whom one report described as eight years old. The killing reached national readers only as a one-sentence item, first under a Vicksburg, Mississippi, dateline and then in weekly news-brief columns.

According to a telegraph dispatch dated Vicksburg, November 3, Andrew Jackson, described as "colored," was "lynched by a mob yesterday," that is, on November 2, "for outraging a white girl." A separately worded brief that ran the following week said that Jackson "had assaulted a little white girl near Vienna, La.," and was "lynched by vigilantes the other day." Another version placed the lynching in Lincoln parish and gave the girl's age as eight.
None of the reports names the girl, gives the number of men involved, says whether Jackson was taken from officers, or describes how he was killed.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Washington Evening Critic printed the Vicksburg item under the headline "Andrew Jackson Lynched." between notices of a dynamite accident and a college bequest, and the Daily Gazette carried the same words among its "Brief Telegrams." From November 8 the Louisiana version circulated in country weeklies, including the Batesville Guard in Arkansas, the St. Landry Democrat in Louisiana and the Grenada Sentinel in Mississippi. The Crawford Avalanche of Grayling, Michigan, ran the Lincoln parish item on November 9 and then, on November 16, the Vicksburg version, which it rendered as a lynching "at Vicksburg, Miss."
Every version stated the accusation as fact and offered no comment on the killing. No Black-press coverage of the episode is available, since the Black-press collection begins in 1900.

The reports disagree on place: the telegraph item carries only a Vicksburg dateline, while the weekly briefs name Vienna and Lincoln Parish, Louisiana. They also differ in calling the killers "a mob" or "vigilantes" and the accuser "a white girl" or "an 8-year-old child."

reader.title: Lynching of Andrew Jackson
bases: Every report says Andrew Jackson, a Black man, was 'lynched' by a 'mob' or by 'vigilantes' over an accusation of assaulting a white girl (A1, A4, A5).

The reports say Jackson was 'lynched by a mob' (A1, A2) or 'by vigilantes' (A4) for outraging or assaulting a white girl (A1, A5); no lawful authority is mentioned, though no report gives the mob's size or the manner of death.

A Vicksburg telegraph item (A1, A2) and a separately worded news-brief item placing the lynching near Vienna, La. (A4, A5) agree that Andrew Jackson was lynched for assaulting a white girl, though they differ on place.

accounts.label: Vicksburg telegraph item
accounts.gist: Andrew Jackson, colored, was lynched by a mob 'yesterday' (Nov. 2) for outraging a white girl; no place other than the Vicksburg dateline is given.

accounts.label: Weekly news-brief item
accounts.gist: Andrew Jackson, a negro who had assaulted a little white girl near Vienna, La., was lynched by vigilantes 'the other day'; another version puts it in Lincoln parish, La., and makes the girl eight years old.

framing.detail: The telegraph item ran under the headline 'Andrew Jackson Lynched.' and in 'Brief Telegrams', stating the charge as fact without comment.
Weekly papers carried the item among 'Crimes and Criminals' or general news briefs, again stating the assault as fact.
